- "Top 20 events by 24h volume across all venues."
- "Events where Polymarket vs Kalshi implied probabilities differ by >10%."

For a deeper dive into the Polymarket‑specific side (Gamma, CLOB, Data v2), see this related guide: [Polymarket API & Gamma Data: What Builders Get and How to Use It in Apps](https://www.codex.io/blog/polymarket-api-and-gamma-data-what-builders-get-and-how-to-use-it-in-apps).

### Latency, Throughput, and Architecture: Where Codex Fits

Venue‑native APIs are optimized for **execution**, not for being your all‑purpose analytics backend. For high‑traffic consumer apps, that matters.

#### Polymarket API latency and throughput constraints

From the docs and rate‑limit tables:

- REST endpoints (Gamma, Data v2, CLOB) are capped at specific requests / 10 seconds
- WebSockets require careful ping/pong and reconnection logic
- Trading latency is bounded by mechanisms like the **150ms crypto taker delay**

If you try to run a [high‑traffic analytics site](https://www.codex.io/blog/polymarket-api-endpoints-gamma-feeds), portfolio tracker, or multi‑venue frontend directly on Polymarket’s REST endpoints, you will:

## NFT Marketplace Onchain Data: Listings, Volume & Price Feeds Product Teams Actually Need

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/nft-listings-feed-api
Published: 2026-10-04
Author: Codex

NFT marketplace product teams need four core onchain data feeds—real-time listings, bids, executed sales, and collection-level floor/volume stats—to power modern discovery, pricing, and portfolio experiences. Instead of building custom indexers across chains and marketplaces, you can plug into infrastructure like Codex to ingest, normalize, and expose these feeds via a single high-performance API.

This guide breaks down the core NFT marketplace data surfaces, then shows how Codex-style onchain APIs let you ship fast without maintaining your own NFT indexing pipeline.

### The Core On-Chain Data Primitives for NFT Marketplaces

For almost every NFT marketplace or NFT-aware product, the same four primitives drive the UI and business logic:

- **Active listings / asks**
- **Active bids / offers**
- **Executed sales / trades**
- **Collection floor price & volume statistics**

OpenSea, Blur, Magic Eden, and others all expose these surfaces in some form via their APIs and streaming endpoints. If you’re building your own marketplace, analytics surface, or social trading app, you need equivalent onchain coverage—preferably across chains and marketplaces, not just your own smart contracts.

Let’s unpack each primitive.

#### 1. NFT Listings Feed API (Active Asks)

An **NFT listings feed API** answers the question: _“What’s currently for sale, at what price, and under what terms?”_

At minimum, you need for each listing:

- NFT identifier (contract, token ID, and collection slug)
- Ask price (in native chain asset and in USD)
- Seller wallet address
- Marketplace / protocol source
- Timestamp and expiration
- Order type (fixed price, Dutch auction, etc.)

Product teams use a listings feed to:

- Populate collection pages and search results
- Highlight best listing per NFT (lowest ask, most recent, or most liquid)
- Display real-time marketplace order books onchain (e.g., all current asks for a collection)

**Codex-style capability:**

- Ingest raw marketplace events (e.g., `OrderCreated`, `ListingAdded`) across chains
- Normalize them into canonical "listing" objects tied to tokens and collections
- Enrich with pricing data (USD equivalent, native-to-USD conversion via trading-grade price feeds)

Because Codex already indexes 80+ networks and 70M+ tokens, the same data infrastructure that powers token order books can be extended to NFTs’ listing views.

#### 2. Real-Time NFT Listings WebSocket (Streaming New Asks)

A **real-time NFT listings WebSocket** or subscription stream answers: _“What just hit the market right now?”_

Polling is too slow and too expensive for serious marketplaces. High-traffic interfaces now rely on:

- **WebSockets** for streaming events
- **GraphQL subscriptions** for fine-grained filters (by collection, wallet, marketplace)
- **Webhooks** for server-side reactions (e.g., alerting, re-ranking, or triggering bots)

Codex’s architectural model is built around this:

- One **GraphQL-style endpoint**
- Query, **subscription**, and **webhook** modes
- Sub-second latencies, optimized specifically for trading- and listing-adjacent UX

For NFTs, this lets you:

- Subscribe to new listings in a collection
- Watch listings from a specific wallet (e.g., whales or curated sellers)
- Stream events into a recommendation engine or activity feed

Instead of standing up your own event decoders and WebSocket gateways per chain, you hook into Codex’s subscriptions and focus on your ranking logic and UI.

#### 3. On-Chain NFT Bids Feed (Active Offers)

An **onchain NFT bids feed** answers: _“Who wants to buy this NFT, at what price, and how does that compare to the asks?”_

For bids/offers, you’ll typically need:

- NFT identifier and collection
- Bid price (native asset + USD)
- Bidder wallet address
- Marketplace or protocol source
- Expiry and any special conditions (e.g., trait-specific bids, collection-wide bids)

This feed powers:

- Best-offer panels on listing pages
- Automated acceptance logic (e.g., instant sale if bid > threshold)
- Liquidity heatmaps per collection or trait

OpenSea’s best-offer endpoints show exactly how product teams think: they want the **current best bid per NFT**, plus history for analytics.

Codex’s generalized “order/trade” schema makes it straightforward to model NFT bids similarly to token limit orders:

- Index bid events across marketplaces
- Tie bids to normalized tokens and wallets
- Surface best bid / full bid ladder per NFT via a single API

#### 4. NFT Sales History API (Executed Trades)

An **NFT sales history API** answers: _“What actually sold, when, and at what price?”_

Key fields for each executed sale:

- NFT identifier and collection
- Sale price in native asset and USD
- Buyer and seller wallets
- Marketplace / protocol source
- Timestamp and transaction hash

You use these feeds to:

- Build price history charts for collections and individual NFTs
- Detect wash-trading and suspicious volume
- Compute time-weighted average prices and trend metrics

As of 2025, DappRadar data shows:

- **18.1M NFTs sold in Q3 2025**, with **$1.58B** trading volume
- **10.1M NFT sales** in October 2025 alone, with **$546M** in volume

Even in a “post-hype” cycle, that’s a lot of onchain activity to index and normalize.

Codex’s pipeline—built for token trades and prediction markets—maps directly:

- Ingest raw NFT trade events from multiple chains and contracts
- Normalize into “trade” entities with buyer/seller and USD prices
- Precompute OHLCV-style aggregates per collection for charting

#### 5. NFT Floor Price API (Collection Stats)

A **NFT floor price API** answers: _“What’s the lowest ask for this collection right now, and how active is it?”_

Almost every marketplace and analytics site exposes floor stats. Typical collection stat surfaces include:

- Floor price (native asset + USD)
- 24h / 7d / 30d volume
- Sales count
- Unique owners / wallets

OpenSea’s collection stats and top-collection endpoints return these metrics, sorted by volume, floor, and sales windows.

Other providers like Alchemy and Bitquery aggregate floor prices across marketplaces. Alchemy’s `getFloorPrice` explicitly returns marketplace-specific floors.

Codex’s edge comes from its **multi-network, normalized aggregates**:

- It already computes **liquidity, volume, holders, and OHLCV** for tokens
- The same infrastructure can compute NFT collection floor, volume, and holder stats
- Because Codex optimizes for **trading-grade accuracy and low latency**, these numbers can safely power ranking, leaderboards, and pricing engines

## 1 BTC, 1 PI, 1 XCH Price Feeds: Designing Stable Single‑Coin Widgets with Onchain Data

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/best-onchain-data-apis-trading-apps-2
Published: 2026-10-03
Author: Codex

Single‑coin price widgets for **1 BTC**, **1 PI**, and **1 XCH** are only "set‑and‑forget" if you design them like production price feeds: clear data sources, deterministic fallbacks, explicit latency and precision rules.

This guide shows how to do that using **Codex** as your primary on‑chain data API and **CEX feeds as fallback**, so you can safely embed widgets into high‑traffic trading and fintech products.

### Why single‑coin widgets are harder than they look

For trading‑adjacent apps, a "simple" 1‑coin widget must handle:

- **Venue fragmentation** (especially for PI and XCH)
- **On‑chain vs CEX price differences**
- **Latency vs finality trade‑offs**
- **Precision, rounding, and UI consistency**

Codex helps by providing:

- **Token‑level prices** (`getTokenPrices`) aggregated across valid DEX pools
- **Pair‑level stats** (`pairMetadata`, `getBars`, `getTokenBars`) for deterministic sources
- **Streaming updates** (`onPriceUpdated`, `onPricesUpdated`, `onTokenBarsUpdated`) for real‑time UX
- **Scalable infra:** 80+ networks, 70M+ tokens, 700M+ wallets, 300 req/s on Growth plan

Your job is to wrap these primitives in a **clear price policy** that works for 1 BTC, 1 PI, and 1 XCH.

### Architecture overview: best on‑chain data APIs for trading apps

For **[high‑traffic trading apps](https://www.codex.io/blog/best-on-chain-data-api-providers)**, the most reliable pattern looks like this:

1. **Primary source: Codex on‑chain aggregates**
   - Use `getTokenPrices` for snapshots and `onPriceUpdated` / `onPricesUpdated` for live streams.
   - Take Codex's **weighted across valid pools** price as the default.
2. **Secondary source: Codex pair‑specific price**
   - Discover liquid pools with `listPairsWithMetadataForToken`.
   - Lock in a stablecoin‑quoted pair (e.g., WBTC/USDC, wrapped PI/USDT proxy) via `pairMetadata` or `getBars`.
3. **Tertiary source: CEX composite price**
   - For **PI** and **XCH**, Codex on‑chain coverage may be limited.
   - Pull quotes from OKX, MEXC, or other active spot venues.
4. **Policy layer: normalization & fallback logic**
   - Normalize each price to a **USD float + precision metadata**.
   - Apply deviation thresholds, latency budgets, and rounding rules.

This pattern gives you:

- Codex as **the primary, unified on‑chain data layer**
- Explicit **fallback routes** per asset
- A **deterministic contract** between backend and widget UI

### Step 1: Define your price model for 1 BTC, 1 PI, 1 XCH

Before touching APIs, specify what "price" means for your widget:

- **Spot price** (best effort, near real‑time)
- **Short TWAP** (e.g., 5–15 min) to smooth micro‑volatility and pool noise
- **Oracle‑style guarded price** (deviation and heartbeat rules)

For single‑coin widgets embedded in apps like wallets, CEXs, or dashboards, a good default is:

- **Display spot‑like price** (Codex aggregate + CEX fallback)
- **Guard with TWAP / deviation checks** behind the scenes

We’ll reuse this model for BTC, PI, and XCH; only the **source graph** differs.

### 1 BTC: normalize BTC and WBTC feeds from on‑chain liquidity pools

For BTC, the issue is **not coverage**, it’s **representation**:

- On‑chain, you usually see **wrapped BTC** (WBTC, CBTC, tBTC, etc.).
- Off‑chain, you have BTC spot markets on major CEXs.

To get a robust 1 BTC price using Codex:

#### 1. Choose your on‑chain BTC proxy

Pick a wrapped asset with deep liquidity on the chain(s) you support, e.g.:

- **Ethereum:** WBTC
- **Solana:** wrapped BTC from a major bridge

Use Codex to discover the most reliable pool:

```
query TopBtcPairs {
  listPairsWithMetadataForToken(
    input: {
      tokenAddress: "<WBTC_ADDRESS>"
      chainId: "ethereum-mainnet"  # example
      limit: 5
    }
  ) {
    pairs {
      pairAddress
      baseToken { address symbol decimals }
      quoteToken { address symbol decimals }
      priceUsd
      liquidityUsd
      volume24hUsd
    }
  }
}
```

Then:

- Filter for **stablecoin quote** (USDC/USDT) pairs.
- Sort by `liquidityUsd` and lock in the top one or two as **approved sources**.

#### 2. Use Codex token‑level aggregates as default

Codex's `getTokenPrices` gives you **aggregate, liquidity‑weighted** prices across valid pools:

```
query BtcPrice {
  getTokenPrices(
    input: {
      tokens: [{
        chainId: "ethereum-mainnet"
        address: "<WBTC_ADDRESS>"
      }]
    }
  ) {
    prices {
      priceUsd
      priceNative
      token { symbol address decimals }
      sourcePairAddress
      updatedAt
    }
  }
}
```

Key points:

- `priceUsd` is a **float** – keep more precise internal representation where needed.
- `sourcePairAddress` indicates the dominant pair used in the aggregate.
- Use `updatedAt` and your own **max age** rule (e.g., 20–30 seconds).

#### 3. Add CEX reference as a guardrail

Kraken, for example, shows BTC at roughly **$84,262** with **$35.51B** 24h volume and WBTC around **$83,419** with **$142.85M** 24h volume.

A simple policy:

- Fetch **BTC/USDT** or **BTC/USD** from 1–2 major CEXs.
- Compute a CEX composite price `p_cex`.
- Compare with Codex aggregate `p_codex`:
  - If `|p_codex − p_cex| / p_cex < 1–2%` → accept `p_codex`.
  - Else → flag **degraded status**, optionally show `p_cex` with a small badge.

This gives you a **defensible 1 BTC price** principally driven by on‑chain data.

### 1 PI: aggregate price feed from CEX and DEX for a fragmented asset

PI is a good example of why **CEX fallback routes** matter:

- OKX has active **PI/USDT** spot with last price ~**0.09162 USDT**, 24h turnover **2.64M USDT** and **28.76M PI** volume.
- Binance displays a PI page with a reference price (~**$0.09156**) but explicitly says PI is **not listed** for trading.

That means your widget must be **venue‑aware**.

#### 1. Check Codex token coverage first

If PI exists as an on‑chain token in your supported networks (e.g., wrapped PI or representations on alt‑chains), start with Codex:

- Use `getTokenPrices` for the PI token address(es).
- If Codex returns **no price or extremely low liquidity**, treat on‑chain data as **insufficient**.

#### 2. Build a CEX‑first composite price

Given PI's fragmented markets, a robust approach is:

1. Select a set of **trusted venues**, e.g. OKX + 1–2 others.
2. For each, stream **PI/USDT** order‑book or ticker updates.
3. Compute `p_cex` as:
   - A **volume‑weighted average** across venues
   - Or a **median** if you want to resist outliers

Normalize everything to USD:

```
p_usd = last_price_pi_usdt * usdt_usd_rate
```

Codex can provide **USDT→USD** conversion using stablecoin token prices, so the whole stack remains anchored in the same data layer.

#### 3. Fall back to Codex if CEX data breaks

If all CEX feeds for PI are stale or down:

- Attempt **on‑chain price discovery** for any wrapped PI you support:
  - `listPairsWithMetadataForToken` → discover PI pairs against stablecoins.
  - `getTokenBars` → get historical bars and compute a short TWAP.
- If liquidity and data look reasonable, use that as a **temporary price** with a degraded indicator.

If both Codex and CEX are compromised, **freeze the last good price** and show a status badge. Explicit failure beats silently wrong prices.

### 1 XCH: unify on‑chain and CEX prices for a niche asset

XCH (Chia) sits between BTC and PI in terms of fragmentation:

- OKX’s **XCH/USDT**: last price ~**1.439 USDT**, 24h turnover **127.8K USDT** and **90.17K XCH**.
- MEXC shows XCH around **$1.634**.
- Kraken and Coinbase show **reference prices** (~$1.60–1.65) but state that XCH is **not tradable** there.

#### 1. Decide chain representation strategy

Depending on your product:

- If you **don't index Chia directly** but support wrapped XCH on EVM or other chains, treat it like BTC:
  - Use Codex for **wrapped XCH tokens** and stablecoin pairs.
  - Guard with CEX XCH/USDT prices.
- If you **do index Chia natively** (outside Codex), you can:
  - Treat your native indexer as another source.
  - Still normalize everything through **Codex stablecoin prices**.

#### 2. Normalize Codex and CEX prices

Process both sources into a common representation:

```
p_codex_usd = codex_price_xch_usd
p_cex_usd   = composite_cex_price_xch_usd
```

Apply a policy similar to BTC:

- Accept Codex if deviation < X% and data is fresh.
- Else prefer `p_cex_usd`, but still **record** Codex values for analytics.

Because XCH markets are thinner than BTC, you may want a **slightly higher deviation threshold** (e.g., 3–5%).

### Latency of on‑chain price feeds vs CEX streams

High‑traffic trading apps care about **how often** prices update and **how risky** those updates are.

Codex offers both **queries** and **subscriptions**:

- `getTokenPrices` / `getTokenBars` → pull at your cadence (e.g., 1–5 seconds for widgets).
- `onPriceUpdated` / `onPricesUpdated` → push updates **at most once per block** per token.
- `onTokenBarsUpdated` → stream bar completion events, defaulting to **confirmed** data.

Key latency design choices:

1. **Delivery mode**
   - For Solana, Codex exposes `processed` mode (lowest latency, reorg risk) vs `confirmed` (safer, slightly slower); see [handling reorgs and finality](https://www.codex.io/blog/blockchain-reorgs-application-data).
   - For most widgets, use **confirmed** charts and quotes; reserve `processed` for pro trading UIs willing to handle reorgs.
2. **Widget update cadence**
   - Price text: update with each subscription event (per‑block cadence is usually enough).
   - Sparkline / micro‑chart: update every **1–2 seconds** to look alive but avoid thrashing.
3. **CEX comparison cadence**
   - CEX order‑books can update as fast as every **10ms** (OKX) or 100ms.
   - You usually don't need that for a widget; **0.5–2 seconds** is sufficient and easier on rate limits.

### Fallback price routes and policy engine design

Instead of ad‑hoc `if/else` logic in widget code, design a **price policy engine**:

#### 1. Explicit source priority per asset

Define for each of 1 BTC, 1 PI, 1 XCH:

- **Source list:** `[Codex_aggregate, Codex_pair, CEX_composite, Last_good]`
- **Priority order** and rules for when to step down.

Example for BTC:

1. `Codex_aggregate` if:
   - `updatedAt` < 30s old AND
   - deviation from `CEX_composite` < 2%.
2. Otherwise `CEX_composite` if fresh (<10s).
3. Otherwise `Last_good` with a stale badge.

#### 2. Deviation and heartbeat thresholds

Borrow from Chainlink’s model:

- **Deviation threshold:** max % difference between sources or between new and last value.
- **Heartbeat:** max time between updates before forcing a refresh.

Example defaults for widgets:

- Deviation: 2% for BTC, 3–5% for PI/XCH.
- Heartbeat: 60s for display, tighter for trading surfaces.

#### 3. Error signaling to the frontend

Standardize status flags your API sends to the widget:

```
{
  "symbol": "BTC",
  "priceUsd": 84262.15,
  "source": "codex_aggregate",
  "deviationPct": 0.4,
  "isStale": false,
  "isDegraded": false,
  "updatedAt": 1753121580
}
```

The widget can then:

- Render a **subtle indicator** when `isDegraded` is true.
- Gray out values or show a tooltip when `isStale` is true.

### Price precision and rounding for crypto widgets

Precision issues are easy to overlook and hard to debug.

#### 1. Respect token decimals and exchange increments

From Codex:

- Tokens expose `decimals`.
- Prices may be floats, but volumes/OHLC are often strings for higher precision.

From CEXs:

- Kraken: `price_increment` and `qty_precision` (e.g., BTC/USD increment 0.1, precision 8).
- Binance: `PRICE_FILTER.tickSize` and `LOT_SIZE.stepSize`.

#### 2. Internal vs display precision

Best practice for **most reliable on‑chain data APIs for trading apps**:

- Internal math:
  - Use **decimal/fixed‑point libraries**.
  - Store prices as integers + explicit decimals where possible.
- Display:
  - BTC: 2 decimal places (e.g., `84,262.15`).
  - PI/XCH: 4–6 decimal places depending on price level.

Only round at the **last possible step** in the UI pipeline.

#### 3. Consistent formatting across sources

Because Codex and CEXs may differ slightly in formatting:

- Normalize everything to a **standard internal representation**:

```
struct PricePoint {
  symbol: string
  value: Decimal // precise
  decimals: int
  source: enum
  updatedAt: timestamp
}
```

- Convert to UI decimals from this struct, not from raw floats.

### Embedding single‑coin widgets in high‑traffic apps

When you embed 1 BTC, 1 PI, or 1 XCH widgets into consumer apps (wallets, CEX apps, social trading, etc.), you must think about scale:

- Codex Growth plan: **300 requests/second** cap.
- **Subscriptions** (`onPricesUpdated`) let you stream up to **25 tokens per call** and reuse connections across widgets.

Implementation tips:

1. **Server‑side aggregation**
   - Run subscriptions **server‑side**.
   - Broadcast normalized prices to clients via your own WebSocket.
2. **Cache and coalesce**
   - Cache latest price per asset per region.
   - Coalesce UI updates into a **max 1–2 updates per second** per widget.
3. **Security and abuse controls**
   - Never expose raw CEX API keys client‑side.
   - Treat Codex as the public‑facing source; CEX is a backend‑only guardrail.

If you’re also working with ADA and other majors, see this related guide on building multi‑asset widgets: [ADA to USD and Top ADA Coin Data: Powering Trading Apps with On‑Chain APIs](https://www.codex.io/blog/ada-to-usd-and-top-ada-coin-data-powering-trading-apps-with-on-chain-apis) and our [ADA price and NFT widget tutorial](https://www.codex.io/blog/ada-usd-api).

### Example: consolidated 1‑coin price API using Codex

A thin Node/TypeScript service for 1 BTC price might:

1. Subscribe to Codex prices:

```
subscription BtcPriceStream {
  onPriceUpdated(
    input: {
      token: {
        chainId: "ethereum-mainnet"
        address: "<WBTC_ADDRESS>"
      }
    }
  ) {
    priceUsd
    updatedAt
    sourcePairAddress
  }
}
```

2. Poll CEX BTC/USDT tickers every 2 seconds.
3. Run the policy engine described above.
4. Expose `/price/BTC` to your frontends with a compact JSON payload.

You can reuse this same shape for PI and XCH with asset‑specific source priority.

By treating 1 BTC, 1 PI, and 1 XCH widgets as **mini price oracles** backed by Codex’s trading‑grade on‑chain data and CEX fallbacks, you get stable, predictable behavior that scales to millions of users without surprise price glitches.

## What Is a Blockchain Analysis Tool?

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/blockchain-analysis-tool-on-chain-api
Published: 2026-10-02
Author: Codex

A **blockchain analysis tool** is software that ingests raw on‑chain activity, aggregates and enriches it into higher‑level entities like wallets, tokens, pools, and markets, and then surfaces those insights through queries or visualizations so product and business teams can make decisions about trading, risk, and user behavior.

### How a Blockchain Analysis Tool Works

At its core, a blockchain analysis tool sits _above_ raw node access. It connects to one or more blockchains, consumes blocks, logs, and events, and normalizes them into a consistent data model. Instead of dealing with per‑chain quirks, engineers query standardized objects: trades, holders, liquidity, OHLC candles, or prediction markets.

In practice, this means three main steps:

1. **Ingest:** Continuously stream and index thousands of transactions per second across many networks.
2. **Enrich:** Turn low‑level events into meaningful entities and metrics (token prices, wallet clusters, liquidity, unique traders, TVL‑like stats).
3. **Serve:** Expose that trading‑grade data via APIs and visual layers—charts, [dashboards, or analytics surfaces](https://www.codex.io/blog/codex-api-integration-looker-metabase-grafana).

Codex is specifically built to power this analysis layer. It ingests and enriches raw blockchain data across **80+ networks**, **700M+ wallets**, and **70M+ tokens**, and exposes it via an all‑in‑one GraphQL‑style API designed for exchanges, wallets, dashboards, and prediction market frontends.

### Why Blockchain Analysis Tools Matter for Product Teams

For web3 and fintech products, the difference between "we have node access" and "we have trading‑grade analytics" is the difference between a prototype and a production app. Raw RPC calls can tell you that a transaction happened; they do not tell you which token it belongs to, how it affected liquidity, or how it changed a trader’s PnL across chains.

Product and engineering teams at exchanges, DeFi dashboards, and prediction market frontends need **real‑time and historical context**, not just events. They care about:

- Live token prices in USD and native units.
- Trading‑ready chart data (candles, OHLC, volume) for every asset they list.
- Wallet‑level behavior: balances, flows, and cross‑chain exposure.
- Prediction market metrics: open interest, liquidity, unique traders, and event states.

Codex’s data APIs turn this into a solved problem. By providing sub‑second latency and **thousands of events per second** throughput, Codex lets teams focus on UX and business logic rather than building and maintaining ETL pipelines, indexers, and enrichment jobs across dozens of chains.

For NFT‑aware products in particular, the same analysis patterns extend to rarity, collection‑level metrics, and holder behavior. A deeper treatment of those NFT‑specific topics appears in the related guide: [Blockchain Data Analytics and Rarity Tools: Building Trading-Grade NFT Insights](https://www.codex.io/blog/blockchain-data-analytics-and-rarity-tools-building-trading-grade-nft-insights).

### How Codex Underpins Blockchain Analysis Tools

A modern blockchain analysis tool typically doesn’t own every part of the data pipeline. Instead, it leans on a specialized **on‑chain data API** that already handles indexing, enrichment, and normalization across networks. Codex is designed to be that upstream layer.

For token and trading analytics, Codex provides:

- **Real‑time and historical prices** in USD and native units.
- **Trading‑ready chart data:** OHLC, candles, and volume across 80+ chains.
- **Aggregated metrics:** liquidity, volume, unique wallets, TVL‑like stats.
- **Holders and balances** across chains, plus scam filtering and token metadata.

For prediction markets, Codex goes further with a unified GraphQL API for **Polymarket** and **Kalshi**. It exposes:

- Events and markets, with states, odds, and settlement details.
- Trades and trader activity, including volume, open interest, and unique traders.
- Ranking signals for dashboards: liquidity, active traders, and market health.

This specialization is trading‑grade. Codex’s docs cite support for **1,000+ requests per second** on prediction‑market endpoints, versus roughly **30 req/s** for Polymarket’s native API and **20 req/s** for Kalshi’s native API. That difference directly affects whether your frontend can handle real traffic spikes when volumes surge—Polymarket reported **$12.7B total volume in September 2026** across its US and International venues.

### Analysis Tools vs Node Providers vs Explorers

Blockchain analysis tools are often confused with node providers and explorers, but they occupy a distinct layer in the stack.

#### Node / RPC Providers

Node providers (sometimes called **blockchain APIs** or RPC services) expose the raw transport layer: blocks, transactions, logs, and state. Examples include services that offer RPC, REST, or gRPC across dozens of chains.

They are essential for chain access, but their outputs are **low‑level**. You still need to parse event logs, decode contract ABIs, correlate addresses, and compute aggregates. For trading apps, this means building your own wallet clustering, entity resolution, and token analytics before you can answer simple questions like "What’s this user’s cross‑chain portfolio value?" or "How did liquidity move after this listing?".

#### Blockchain Explorers

[Explorers like Blockscout](https://www.codex.io/blog/polygon-block-explorer-api) are **human‑facing frontends** that index and organize chain data into searchable pages. They make it easy for an individual user to inspect a transaction, token, or address.

However, explorers are not optimized for **high‑volume programmatic access** or multi‑chain analytics. They don’t typically provide sub‑second, trading‑grade APIs for:

- Streaming chart data into a live order book.
- Computing aggregate metrics across thousands of markets.
- Running portfolio‑level analytics across 700M+ wallets.

#### Blockchain Analysis Tools

A blockchain analysis tool, by contrast, is **application‑facing**. It uses node or data APIs as inputs, then adds:

- Cross‑chain indexing and normalization.
- Enrichment into domain‑specific objects (tokens, pools, NFTs, markets).
- Aggregation, clustering, and wallet‑ or trader‑level analytics.
- Query layers and visualizations optimized for product teams.

Codex sits squarely in this analysis layer, even though it exposes its capabilities as an API rather than a GUI. Its own framing is that "most blockchain data APIs start from node RPCs and expose lightly processed logs," which works for explorers and hobby dashboards but **breaks for trading UIs, portfolio dashboards, market‑making, and prediction‑market frontends**. Codex bridges that gap by delivering enriched, trading‑ready data.

## What Is a Trace Transaction API? Deep Onchain Call Trees for Product Teams

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/trace-transaction-api-call-tree
Published: 2026-10-01
Author: Codex

A trace transaction API is a blockchain data interface that returns the full internal execution trace of a transaction—its nested call tree, subcalls, reverts, state changes, and value flows—rather than just the top-level receipt and emitted events. It exposes how a transaction actually executed inside the virtual machine, including internal token transfers, gas usage, and which addresses and storage slots were touched.

### How a Trace Transaction API Works

At the client level, tracing a transaction means re‑executing it with an attached tracer that records every internal step. Geth, for example, notes that a trace may require re‑running all preceding transactions in the same block and earlier blocks until the last stored snapshot, which is why trace workloads are materially heavier than simple `eth_getTransactionReceipt` calls.

The tracer builds an ordered call tree of the execution. Methods like `debug_traceTransaction` (QuickNode values this at 40 credits versus 20 credits for a standard receipt) or trace APIs from Alchemy and Chainstack return a structured view of:

- The full internal call hierarchy (`call`, `delegatecall`, `staticcall`, `create`)
- Revert points and error reasons
- Gas used at each step
- Token and value movements inside the transaction, not just surface transfers

Codex sits on top of this raw trace output, ingesting and enriching traces across 80+ networks and 700M+ wallets. Instead of exposing opaque opcode logs, Codex normalizes traces into trading‑ready objects—classified swaps, liquidations, bridges, and other contract‑mediated actions—so product teams can query them via a single high‑performance API.

### Why Trace Transaction APIs Matter for Product Teams

Standard RPC receipts and event logs are optimized for efficiency, not explainability. Ethereum receipts expose status and logs, but as Geth explicitly states, they do not reveal “what was modified and which addresses were touched.” That missing detail becomes a critical blind spot for trading‑adjacent products.

For Web3 and fintech builders, the core value of a trace transaction API is categorization. With full internal call trees and fund flows, you can reliably distinguish:

- A simple ERC‑20 transfer from a routed multi‑hop DEX swap
- A normal borrow/repay from a liquidation sequence
- A straightforward send from a bridge hop or cross‑chain messaging pattern
- A direct call from a proxy or `delegatecall` pattern that routes through multiple contracts

This is especially important for Codex’s customers: high‑traffic trading apps, exchanges, wallets, and analytics platforms that need to show _what_ happened in [a wallet’s history](https://www.codex.io/blog/wallet-transaction-history-api-design), not just _that_ something happened. When your app powers millions of users and real money decisions, mis‑classifying a liquidation as a simple transfer or failing to surface an internal token movement is unacceptable.

Codex uses trace transaction APIs to build enriched, production‑ready datasets: trading‑grade chart data, aggregated liquidity and volume, cross‑chain holders, and prediction market analytics. Because traces expose all internal token movements and calls, Codex can correctly attribute swaps, fees, MEV‑adjacent behaviors, and prediction market trades, even when they are deeply nested inside meta‑transactions. For a deeper overview of how these requirements play out in wallet UX and infra design, see this related guide: Wallet Transaction History and Trace Transaction APIs: Data Requirements for Web3 Products.

### Related Terms and How Trace APIs Differ

Trace transaction APIs are often confused with standard RPC and event‑log interfaces. In practice, they solve a different problem.

#### Trace Transaction API vs Standard RPC

Standard RPC methods like `eth_getTransactionReceipt` and `eth_getTransactionByHash` return high‑level information: status, gas used, logs, and basic metadata. They are cheap to query and sufficient for many simple integrations, but they do not expose the internal execution tree or state deltas.

By contrast, a trace transaction API replays the transaction with a tracer (e.g., Geth’s `callTracer` or `structLogger`) and returns the full call hierarchy and internal value flows. Providers such as QuickNode and Alchemy document these as `debug_traceTransaction` or `trace_transaction` methods, clearly distinguishing them from regular RPC because of their higher compute cost and richer output.

For product teams [building trading interfaces](https://www.codex.io/blog/on-chain-data-api-prediction-market-frontends), the practical difference is this: standard RPC tells you _that_ a swap happened; trace APIs tell you _how_ it happened, _through which contracts_, and _which assets moved where_ at every step. Codex leverages the latter to ensure its aggregates and classifications are correct across 70M+ tokens and 80+ networks.

#### Trace Transaction API vs Event Logs

Event logs are emitted by contracts using `emit` statements. They are index‑friendly and essential for many workflows, but they only capture what contracts choose to log. Ethereum.org’s logging documentation emphasizes that logs don’t show the entire call graph or all state transitions.

A trace transaction API, on the other hand, records every internal call and state touch regardless of whether the contract logs it. OWASP’s smart‑contract forensics material shows why this matters: reconstructing an exploit or liquidation chain requires internal calls and opcode‑level state transitions that receipts and logs alone cannot provide.

For Codex, logs remain necessary but insufficient. Trace + logs together form the backbone of its enriched data: traces reveal the full execution path; logs provide explicit semantic markers. Codex merges both into a single normalized view so your app can treat complex DeFi flows as simple “swap,” “liquidation,” or “bridge” objects.

### Example: Categorizing a Complex DeFi Swap with Trace Data

Consider a user executing a seemingly straightforward DEX swap: swapping USDC for a long‑tail token via a router contract. From a surface perspective, you might only see one transaction from the user’s wallet to the router, plus a few logs.

Using only standard RPC receipts and logs, the wallet UI can show that USDC left the wallet and another token arrived. However, it may not be able to reliably infer whether this was:

- A single‑pool swap on one DEX
- A multi‑hop route across two or three pools
- A cross‑DEX aggregation through a meta‑router
- A partial swap with leftover tokens refunded

With a trace transaction API, Codex can see the entire internal call tree:

- The user calls the router contract
- The router calls DEX A’s pool contract
- The router then calls DEX B’s pool for a second hop
- The router pays protocol fees to a fee collector contract
- A small refund is sent back to the user

The trace also exposes internal value flows—for example, USDC moving from the user to pool A, intermediate tokens moving between pools, and the final asset moving from the router to the user. Tenderly’s productized execution views and Alchemy’s description of “whole trace trees” illustrate this kind of decoded perspective.

Codex ingests that trace, decodes the contracts involved, and classifies the transaction as a “multi‑hop swap via router,” attaching structured attributes such as:

- Route composition (DEX A → DEX B)
- Pools touched and effective prices
- Protocol and LP fees
- Slippage and final execution price

For a trading app or wallet built on Codex, this means a user’s history can display a single, clear entry like:

> “Swapped 1,000 USDC for 950 TOKENX via RouterXYZ (2 pools, total fee 0.3%).”

Behind that simple sentence sits a complex call tree and multiple internal transfers that only a trace transaction API can surface. The product team didn’t have to [build or maintain trace infrastructure](https://www.codex.io/blog/onchain-data-apis-trading-apps) themselves; Codex did the heavy lifting across all supported chains.

The same pattern applies to liquidations and bridge hops. Internal calls reveal when a position was force‑closed, which collateral was seized, and how it was routed through liquidity venues; or how assets moved across L1, L2, or rollups. Codex uses trace APIs to convert those low‑level flows into high‑level events so your trading interface, portfolio view, or prediction market frontend can stay accurate at scale.

In short, a trace transaction API is the foundation for deep on‑chain explainability. It transforms raw execution into structured insight, and when paired with Codex’s enrichment layer, it becomes a single, trading‑grade data source that product teams can plug into instead of building fragile tracing and ETL pipelines themselves.

## What Is a Crypto Exchange API? Data Interfaces for Trading-Grade Products

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/crypto-exchange-api-trading-data
Published: 2026-09-30
Author: Codex

A **crypto exchange API** is the set of programmatic endpoints a centralized or decentralized exchange exposes for orders, market data, account information, and sometimes onchain events, allowing developers to integrate trading and portfolio functionality directly into their products.

### How a Crypto Exchange API Works for High‑Traffic Trading Apps

At a high level, a crypto exchange API gives your product two core surfaces:

- **Trading endpoints** for submitting, canceling, and managing orders, plus viewing positions and balances.
- **Market data endpoints** for prices, order books, trades, and sometimes funding and derivatives data.

Major exchanges such as Coinbase, Binance, and Kraken typically split these into REST or FIX order entry APIs and **WebSocket feeds** for real-time market data and order/account updates. Coinbase, for example, offers REST, FIX Order Entry, WebSocket market data, and FIX Market Data so different trading workflows can match their latency and reliability needs.

For high-traffic consumer apps and trading terminals, engineers usually:

- Use **REST/FIX** for deterministic operations (orders, withdrawals, account changes).
- Use **WebSockets** for streaming prices, order book depth, and trade ticks at low latency.

This architecture lets you keep execution tightly coupled to the venue while still exposing rich trading features in your own front end.

For a deeper systems view of how exchange APIs fit into modern market data stacks, see [TradingView API and Crypto Exchange APIs: Building High-Throughput Market Data Stacks](https://www.codex.io/blog/tradingview-api-and-crypto-exchange-apis-building-high-throughput-market-data-st).

### Why a Crypto Exchange API Matters for Trading‑Grade Products

If your product touches live trading or portfolio views, a crypto exchange API is the **source of truth for execution and venue-native data**.

Product and engineering teams rely on it to:

- **Execute trades safely:** authenticated endpoints guarantee orders and balances match the venue.
- **Mirror the live order book:** WebSocket feeds let you show depth, spreads, and recent trades in real time.
- **Support derivatives and advanced products:** APIs surface futures, options, and margin data with consistent semantics.

However, an exchange API only covers **its own venue**. It won’t give you:

- Cross-chain token prices and holders.
- Long-tail token discovery across 80+ networks.
- Onchain liquidity and prediction market data.

That’s where a specialized onchain data layer like **Codex** complements exchange connectivity (see [augmenting exchange APIs with onchain data](https://www.codex.io/blog/best-crypto-exchange-apis-on-chain)).

Platforms like **Polymarket** and **Kalshi** expose their own APIs for creating, trading, and settling markets on events (e.g., elections, macro indicators). These prediction market APIs include:

- Market discovery and metadata.
- Order books and trades for event contracts.
- User positions and settlement information.

Codex’s **prediction market data endpoints** index these markets at scale, providing a unified onchain data API for prediction markets. ### Crypto Exchange APIs vs. Blockchain Data APIs vs. Charting SDKs

A crypto exchange API is often confused with other data tools. The distinctions matter when you’re building high-throughput systems.

#### Crypto Exchange API vs. Blockchain Data API

A **crypto exchange API** is venue-specific and focuses on **orders, venue market data, and account information**.

A **blockchain data API** (such as Codex or The Graph) indexes **raw onchain activity across many networks** and turns it into entities like tokens, balances, swaps, holders, and chart-ready price feeds.

In practice:

- Use the **exchange API** for execution and order book data at a specific CEX or DEX.
- Use the **onchain data API** for cross-chain token intelligence, long-tail assets, wallets, and prediction markets.

#### Crypto Exchange API vs. Charting SDK

A **charting SDK** (like TradingView’s Charting Library) is a **UI component**, not a data source. It expects you to plug in a backend **datafeed** that supplies historical candles and live bars.

The crypto exchange API and onchain data API provide the **datafeed**; the charting SDK renders it. TradingView’s docs explicitly state that you must implement asynchronous callbacks to deliver market data from your own infrastructure.

So:

- **Exchange API:** trading and venue data.
- **Onchain data API:** multi-chain token and prediction market intelligence.
- **Charting SDK:** front-end visualization layer that consumes both.

## What Is a Prediction Market Data API? Odds, Liquidity and Resolution Feeds

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/prediction-market-data-api-odds-liquidity
Published: 2026-09-29
Author: Codex

A prediction market data API is a machine-readable interface that exposes prediction events, markets, order books, odds (implied probabilities), liquidity, trading activity, and resolution outcomes from platforms like Polymarket and Kalshi so builders can power odds dashboards, trading terminals, and analytics apps without building their own data pipelines.

### How a Prediction Market Data API Works

At its core, a prediction market data API organizes information around **events** and **markets**. An event represents a real-world question (for example, "US recession by end of 2026?") and can contain one or multiple outcome markets. Each market has its own price, order book, and liquidity profile.

Prices in prediction markets are quoted as **implied probabilities**. On Polymarket, for instance, contracts trade between **$0.01 and $0.99**, where the price corresponds to the market’s probability of resolving "Yes." When the event resolves, the winning side pays out $1 per share and the losing side goes to $0.

A robust prediction market data API therefore does much more than return a single price. It typically exposes:

- **Discovery data:** lists of events and markets, with categories, tags, and filters.
- **Market data:** odds, last trade, daily volume, total volume, liquidity, and open interest.
- **Order books:** resting bids and asks, depth at each price level, and spread.
- **Trade feeds:** individual trades with timestamp, side, size, and participant identifiers.
- **Resolution state:** outcome, resolution time, and settlement details.

Codex mirrors the way platforms like Polymarket structure their own APIs, but normalizes data into a **single GraphQL-style schema**. For example, Codex’s `predictionMarketBars` returns OHLC price data plus volume, trades, unique traders, liquidity, bid/ask, and open interest, which is exactly what trading UIs and analytics dashboards need.

### Why It Matters for Odds Dashboards and Trading Apps

For Codex’s customers—CTOs, lead engineers, and product teams building trading-adjacent UX—the key value of a prediction market data API is that it adds a **probability layer** on top of the crypto economy. Instead of just token prices, apps can show what the market thinks about elections, macro events, sports, and protocol milestones.

Platform pages like Polymarket’s "All Predictions" make this demand obvious. As of **September 27, 2026**, Polymarket lists **7,313 live markets**, each with real-time odds, liquidity, daily volume, and resolution status. Builders creating odds dashboards, social trading tools, or portfolio views need to ingest and rank thousands of markets in real time.

Doing that directly from raw chain data is essentially impossible for most product teams. They would need to:

- Index event and market contracts for each protocol.
- Reconstruct order books and trade history.
- Track resolution outcomes and settlement.
- Maintain schema differences across multiple venues.

Codex’s prediction market data API abstracts all of this away. Engineering teams plug into Codex and immediately get:

- **Trading-grade latency** for odds and order books.
- **Unified endpoints** for events, markets, trades, and charts across Polymarket and Kalshi.
- **Rich ranking signals** like trending score, volume, liquidity, open interest, trades, and unique traders across multiple time windows (5m, 1h, 4h, 12h, 24h, 1w).

This is critical for [high-traffic odds dashboards and trading interfaces](https://www.codex.io/blog/prediction-market-api-frontend-realtime-data) where every millisecond and every correct data point matters. Codex’s infrastructure has already been proven at scale by powering apps like Coinbase, TradingView, Uniswap, Magic Eden, Rainbow, and others.

### How It Differs from General Price Feeds

Prediction market data APIs are often confused with generic **price feeds** or **crypto data APIs**, but they serve a different job.

A typical price feed (for example, a token price API) focuses on:

- Spot prices and OHLC candles for assets.
- Market-wide volume and liquidity metrics.
- Token metadata and possibly holders and balances.

These feeds are ideal for wallets, DeFi dashboards, and portfolio apps. However, they do **not** natively understand the structure of prediction markets: events, outcome tokens, negative-risk groups, and resolution logic.

By contrast, a prediction market data API must:

- Model **events** and their related **markets**, not just assets.
- Track **resolution outcomes** and settlement (which markets pay $1 and which pay $0).
- Provide **order book context** (bids, asks, depth) and implied odds.
- Support **trader analytics**, such as trades and unique traders in a market.

Polymarket’s own docs highlight this distinction. They split their surfaces into **Gamma discovery**, **CLOB market data**, **analytics**, and **WebSocket streams**—underscoring that prediction market infra is about much more than price quotes.

Codex reflects this by exposing dedicated endpoints like `predictionEvents`, `predictionMarkets`, `predictionTrades`, and `predictionMarketBars`. This yields a complete view of **what question is being asked**, **what odds the market assigns**, **how much capital is at risk**, and **how exactly traders are interacting with the market**.

For Codex’s customers, the practical outcome is clear: you use Codex’s token and onchain data APIs for portfolios, charts, and balances; and you use Codex’s prediction APIs when you need **live odds, market context, and resolution feeds** integrated into the same app.

### Related Terms and Common Confusions

Several terms sit near "prediction market data API" and are easy to mix up. It helps to be precise:

#### Prediction Market API vs. Prediction Market Data API

A **prediction market API** can encompass both data and **execution** (placing orders, creating markets, managing accounts). Platform-native APIs from Polymarket or Kalshi often include REST or WebSocket surfaces for both data and trading.

A **prediction market data API** is narrower: it focuses on the **read-only data layer**—events, markets, odds, order books, liquidity, trades, and resolution outcomes. Codex’s prediction endpoints are designed as a data API, not an execution layer, so they are ideal for analytics, dashboards, and trading front-ends that connect to venue-specific execution separately.

#### Price Oracle vs. Prediction Market Data API

A **price oracle** (for example, a DeFi oracle onchain) provides canonical price data to smart contracts. It is optimized for security, decentralization, and onchain consumption.

A **prediction market data API** is off-chain and optimized for **UX and analytics**, not onchain settlement. It’s about powering charts, rankings, and odds displays for human traders and consumer apps.

#### Crypto Market Data API vs. Prediction Market Data API

A **crypto market data API** focuses on standard assets: spot tokens, futures, and maybe options, with endpoints for candles, trades, and order books.

A **prediction market data API** focuses on **event-linked outcome tokens**, resolution mechanics, and implied probabilities—an extra semantic layer that general asset feeds do not handle.

### Example: Powering a Polymarket-Based Frontend with Codex

To make this concrete, consider a team building a **[Polymarket odds dashboard](https://www.codex.io/blog/polymarket-api-endpoints-gamma-feeds)** and market-detail pages using Codex.

They want to:

- Show a scrollable list of top prediction markets by **liquidity** and **volume**.
- Display market cards with **current odds**, **total volume**, and **daily volume**.
- Offer detail pages with **charts**, **recent trades**, and **order book depth**.
- Surface **resolution status** when events close.

Here’s how they could use Codex’s prediction market data API:

1. **Discover and rank events and markets**
   The frontend calls Codex’s event or market filters (for example, `filterPredictionMarkets`) to pull live markets from Polymarket. They can rank by **volume**, **liquidity**, **open interest**, **trades**, or **unique traders** across multiple windows.
2. **Render cards with odds and liquidity**
   For each market, Codex returns current price (implied probability), total volume, daily volume, and liquidity. This mirrors what Polymarket’s own pages show—for example, a single market like **"US recession by end of 2026?"** has generated **$2.2M** in total trading volume.
3. **Build trading-ready charts**
   On the market detail view, the app calls `predictionMarketBars` to get OHLC candles plus volume, trades count, unique traders, liquidity, bid/ask, and open interest over time. This powers an interface similar to a trading terminal, but oriented around event probabilities.
4. **Show trade history and trader activity**
   The app uses `predictionTrades` to list recent trades, including trade type, maker, traderId, priceUsd, amountUsd, timestamp, transaction hash, protocol, and market context. This gives users more insight into how the crowd is moving odds.
5. **Handle resolution and settlement state**
   When events resolve, Codex’s data layer reflects the resolution state: which outcome token redeemed for $1, and which became worthless. The frontend can update the UI to mark markets as **resolved**, highlight the winning outcome, and archive historical performance.

All of this is delivered via Codex’s unified GraphQL-style API, so engineers don’t have to juggle Polymarket’s separate Gamma discovery, CLOB data, analytics, and WebSocket endpoints. For a deeper look at Polymarket’s native APIs and how Codex sits on top of them, see our in-depth guide: [Polymarket API and Gamma Data: What Builders Get and How to Use It in Apps](https://www.codex.io/blog/polymarket-api-and-gamma-data-what-builders-get-and-how-to-use-it-in-apps).

By relying on Codex as the onchain and prediction data layer, teams can focus on UX, ranking logic, and differentiated features—while Codex handles the complexity of indexing, normalizing, and serving **trading-grade prediction market data** across venues.

## How to Design Wallet History APIs for Trading-Grade Web3 Wallets and Dashboards

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/wallet-transaction-history-api-design
Published: 2026-09-28
Author: Codex

### How to Design Wallet History APIs for Trading-Grade Web3 Wallets and Dashboards

By the end of this tutorial, you’ll have a concrete blueprint for a **trading‑grade wallet history API** that:

- Merges on‑chain transactions, internal calls, token transfers, NFTs, and prices into a single timeline
- Uses **cursor‑based pagination** that doesn’t break when new blocks land
- Streams **real‑time updates** without running your own indexers
- Leverages **Codex’s enriched wallet and event feeds** instead of parsing raw chain data

This is a hands‑on, implementation‑first guide for engineering and product teams building Web3 wallets, trading dashboards, and portfolio apps.

If you want a deeper conceptual overview of requirements (PnL, [trace APIs](https://www.codex.io/blog/trace-transaction-api-call-tree), token metadata, etc.), see the related in‑depth guide: Wallet Transaction History and Trace Transaction APIs: Data Requirements for Web3 Products.

### Prerequisites

Before you start implementing, you should have:

- **Technical stack**
  - Backend in Node.js, Python, Go, or similar
  - A database (Postgres, MySQL, or a document store) for local caching and user‑specific state
  - HTTP client and WebSocket client libraries
- **Codex access**
  - A Codex API key (sign up at [codex.io](https://www.codex.io/))
  - Ability to make GraphQL requests (Codex exposes an all‑in‑one GraphQL‑style API)
- **Product requirements defined**
  - Which chains you support today and in the next 6–12 months
  - Whether you need **cross‑chain** timelines per user
  - Whether you show **PnL, cost basis, and performance charts** in the UI

### 1. Define Your Wallet History Requirements as a Merge Problem

A wallet history is **not** a single endpoint. It is a **merge layer** that combines multiple data sources into one ordered timeline.

#### Decide what “history” means for your product

At minimum, trading‑grade timelines should include:

- Native transfers (e.g., ETH, SOL)
- Token transfers (ERC‑20, SPL, etc.)
- Swaps and DEX trades
- NFT mints, transfers, sales
- Protocol interactions (staking, bridging, lending)
- Fiat on/off‑ramp activity (where applicable)

Codex’s wallet and event APIs already expose these as normalized objects with:

- Token metadata (name, symbol, decimals, logos)
- Price at time of trade (USD and native)
- Event types (swap, mint, burn, transfer, etc.)
- Resolved identity and labels

**Actionable design:**

Create a **unified internal event type** that everything maps to, for example:

```
// TypeScript example: your internal wallet event schema

export type WalletEventType =
  | "transfer_in"
  | "transfer_out"
  | "swap"
  | "nft_trade"
  | "bridge"
  | "stake"
  | "unstake"
  | "airdrop";

export interface WalletHistoryEvent {
  id: string;                 // opaque ID from provider + your suffix
  walletAddress: string;
  chainId: string;            // e.g. 'eth-mainnet', 'solana-mainnet'
  timestamp: string;          // ISO-8601
  blockNumber: string;
  txHash: string;
  eventType: WalletEventType;

  // Financials
  amountNative?: string;
  amountUsd?: string;
  feeNative?: string;
  feeUsd?: string;

  // Assets
  tokenIn?: TokenRef;
  tokenOut?: TokenRef;
  nfts?: NftRef[];

  // Enrichment
  priceAtExecutionUsd?: string;
  realizedPnlUsd?: string;
  counterpartyLabel?: string;
  protocolLabel?: string;
  sourcePlatform?: string;    // e.g. 'Uniswap', 'Magic Eden', 'Polymarket'
}

export interface TokenRef {
  address: string;
  chainId: string;
  symbol: string;
  decimals: number;
}

export interface NftRef {
  contractAddress: string;
  tokenId: string;
  collectionName?: string;
}
```

**Common failure:** starting with your provider’s raw response schema and leaking it into your API. That makes it hard to switch vendors or add new event types. Instead, treat Codex (or any provider) as a **source** that you normalize into your own `WalletHistoryEvent` shape.

### 2. Choose Cursor‑Based Pagination From Day One

For trading‑grade UX, pagination is not a detail — it’s a contract.

Offset pagination (`page=2&limit=50`) breaks when:

- New blocks insert events at the **top** of the feed
- [Chain reorgs](https://www.codex.io/blog/blockchain-reorgs-application-data) reorder or remove transactions
- Your filters change (e.g., hiding spam tokens)

#### Use opaque cursors in your API

Codex’s event queries already use [**cursor pagination**](https://www.codex.io/blog/on-chain-data-api-pagination). Cursors are opaque tokens that encode position in the stream and survive inserts.

**Design your public API like this:**

```
GET /v1/wallets/{walletAddress}/history?cursor=opaqueCursor123&limit=50
```

**Example JSON response:**

```
{
  "items": [
    { "id": "evt_1", "eventType": "swap", "timestamp": "2026-09-26T10:00:00Z" },
    { "id": "evt_2", "eventType": "transfer_in", "timestamp": "2026-09-26T09:59:10Z" }
  ],
  "nextCursor": "opaqueCursor124",
  "prevCursor": "opaqueCursor122",
  "hasMore": true
}
```

You can **directly reuse** Codex’s cursor in most cases. If you want abstraction from vendor specifics:

- Store `providerCursor` in your DB
- Issue your own `nextCursor` tokens (e.g., signed JWT or UUID mapping to a row that holds the provider cursor)

**Common failure:** mixing page‑based and cursor‑based pagination across endpoints. Pick **cursor only** for all wallet history APIs, including NFT activity and cross‑chain views.

### 3. Model the Query Layer: One Endpoint, Multiple Sources

Your frontend should call **one wallet history endpoint**. Internally, that endpoint can fan out to different Codex queries depending on filters and time ranges.

#### Example: backend route definition

```
// Pseudo-code Express/Node route

app.get("/v1/wallets/:address/history", async (req, res) => {
  const { address } = req.params;
  const { cursor, limit = 50, chains, types } = req.query;

  const result = await walletHistoryService.fetchTimeline({
    address,
    cursor: cursor as string | undefined,
    limit: Number(limit),
    chains: (chains as string | undefined)?.split(","),
    types: (types as string | undefined)?.split(","),
  });

  res.json(result);
});
```

#### Inside `walletHistoryService.fetchTimeline`

Use Codex queries such as:

- `walletEvents` (or a filtered token/NFT event query)
- `detailedWalletStats` for high‑level info and PnL windows
- `walletChart` for performance charts

A simplified GraphQL request to Codex might look like:

```
query WalletEvents($address: String!, $cursor: String, $limit: Int) {
  walletEvents(
    address: $address
    cursor: $cursor
    limit: $limit
  ) {
    items {
      id
      chainId
      timestamp
      txHash
      eventType
      amountNative
      amountUsd
      tokenIn { address symbol decimals }
      tokenOut { address symbol decimals }
      priceAtExecutionUsd
      realizedPnlUsd
      protocolLabel
    }
    nextCursor
  }
}
```

Map each Codex item into your internal `WalletHistoryEvent` type. For example, map Codex’s `eventType` to your own `WalletEventType` enum.

**Common failure:** exposing multiple endpoints (e.g., `/transactions`, `/swaps`, `/nfts`) and merging on the client. That increases network chatter, complicates pagination, and makes vendor switching harder.

### 4. Normalize and Deduplicate Events Across Chains

Trading‑grade timelines must be **consistent** across 80+ networks, not just Ethereum.

Codex gives you a head start here: it already normalizes token metadata and event types across 80+ chains and 2B+ wallets. But you still need a thin normalization layer.

#### Deduplication strategy

You may see the same logical event via:

- A transaction trace
- A token transfer
- An NFT market event

Define a stable deduplication key, for example:

```
const dedupeKey = `${chainId}:${txHash}:${logIndex || 0}:${subType || ""}`;
```

Store processed keys in a local cache (Redis) or DB table to avoid double‑rendering the same event.

#### Cross‑chain representation

Normalize chain IDs to your own canonical list:

```
// Example mapping

const CHAIN_MAP: Record<string, string> = {
  "1": "eth-mainnet",
  "137": "polygon-mainnet",
  "solana-mainnet": "solana-mainnet",
};
```

Every event you expose should have a `chainId` from this list. That allows:

- Cross‑chain filters in your UI
- Efficient per‑chain caching strategies

**Common failure:** using raw chain identifiers from multiple vendors (e.g., `1`, `ethereum_mainnet`, `ETHEREUM`). This makes filters and analytics buggy and brittle.

### 5. Attach Prices, PnL, and Performance Windows

Trading apps live and die on **PnL correctness**. Users expect:

- Cost basis per position
- Realized profit and loss
- Performance over 1D / 1W / 1M / 1Y windows

Codex exposes this out of the box via endpoints like `detailedWalletStats` and `walletChart`, with:

- PnL windows (1D/1W/1M/1Y)
- Chart data at resolutions like `60`, `240`, `1D`, `7D`
- Metrics such as `volumeUsd`, `realizedProfitUsd`, `swaps`

#### Example: enrich history with stats

Your wallet history endpoint can optionally include a `summary` block:

```
{
  "summary": {
    "wallet": "0xabc...",
    "totalVolumeUsd1D": "15023.45",
    "realizedProfitUsd1W": "-204.18",
    "tradeCount1M": 132
  },
  "events": [ /* ...your events... */ ]
}
```

Fetch `summary` from Codex’s wallet stats / chart endpoints in parallel with the timeline events, and stitch the results before returning.

**Common failure:** computing PnL in‑house from raw trades and prices for every user. This is expensive and error‑prone. Use Codex’s enriched stats as the **source of truth** and only add thin product‑specific logic on top.

### 6. Split Historical Backfill From Real‑Time Tail Updates

High‑traffic wallets and dashboards need **instant initial load** plus **near real‑time updates**.

Codex recommends using:

- **Queries** for one‑time fetches and historical backfill
- **Subscriptions** for live streaming updates
- **Webhooks** for backend notifications and background jobs

#### Architecture pattern

1. **Initial page load**
   - Client calls your `/wallets/:address/history` endpoint
   - Backend fetches from Codex (GraphQL query) and returns first page + cursors
2. **Live updates**
   - Backend subscribes to Codex wallet/event subscriptions per wallet or per address pattern
   - On new event, backend:
     - Normalizes to `WalletHistoryEvent`
     - Updates your cache/DB
     - Pushes via WebSocket or Server‑Sent Events to clients subscribed to that wallet
3. **Webhooks for heavy work**
   - Set up Codex webhooks to notify your backend of large events (e.g., high‑value trades, whales)
   - Trigger background processing (notifications, risk checks, etc.)

**Common failure:** polling the provider every few seconds for each wallet. This causes rate‑limit issues and unnecessary load, and still produces slower UX than subscriptions + webhooks.

### 7. Design Around Vendor Risk With an Abstraction Layer

Vendor continuity is now a real requirement. When SimpleHash shut down its Token API, The Graph launched a Token API specifically to preserve continuity for wallets and explorers. The lesson: [**assume providers can change**](https://www.codex.io/blog/migrate-zerion-to-codex-without-downtime).

#### Introduce an internal provider interface

Define an interface that your application talks to, and implement Codex (and optionally a fallback provider) behind it.

```
export interface WalletHistoryProvider {
  fetchEvents(params: {
    address: string;
    cursor?: string;
    limit: number;
  }): Promise<{ events: WalletHistoryEvent[]; nextCursor?: string }>;

  fetchStats(address: string): Promise<WalletStatsSummary>;
}
```

Codex implementation:

```
export class CodexWalletHistoryProvider implements WalletHistoryProvider {
  constructor(private readonly codexClient: CodexGraphQLClient) {}

  async fetchEvents(params: { address: string; cursor?: string; limit: number }) {
    const { address, cursor, limit } = params;
    const response = await this.codexClient.query(WALLET_EVENTS_QUERY, {
      address,
      cursor,
      limit,
    });

    const events = response.walletEvents.items.map(mapCodexToWalletEvent);

    return {
      events,
      nextCursor: response.walletEvents.nextCursor,
    };
  }

  async fetchStats(address: string): Promise<WalletStatsSummary> {
    // call Codex detailedWalletStats + walletChart here
  }
}
```

Your HTTP handlers talk only to `WalletHistoryProvider`, not to Codex directly.

**Common failure:** tightly coupling your REST or GraphQL schema to one vendor’s response format. That makes migration painful and slows you down when adding new features.

### 8. Implement Caching and Latency Budgets for Trading‑Grade UX

Trading‑adjacent products care deeply about **sub‑second latency** and high uptime. Codex highlights sub‑200ms hot‑cache reads for holdings and balances and targets near‑99.99% uptime for trading‑grade data.

#### Practical caching strategies

- **Short‑lived in‑memory cache** (e.g., 1–5 seconds) for wallet history pages for extremely hot wallets
- **Per‑cursor caching** – cache results keyed by `wallet + cursor` so the “Back” button and infinite scroll feel instant
- **Chain‑aware TTLs** – shorter TTLs for fast chains (e.g., Solana) where new events land quickly; longer TTLs for slower networks

Example cache keying:

```
const cacheKey = `walletHistory:${walletAddress}:${cursor || "root"}:${limit}`;
```

#### Latency budget

Aim for:

- 200–400 ms backend processing time for cached data
- <1s cold path including Codex query + normalization + network latency

**Common failure:** trying to cache per‑transaction forever. Wallet timelines are dynamic — filters, labels, and PnL can change as prices update. Keep caches small and short‑lived; rely on Codex’s own indexing and enrichment for most heavy lifting.

### 9. Add Test Coverage and Edge‑Case Handling

High‑traffic wallets and dashboards need predictable behavior in edge cases.

#### Edge cases to cover

- Wallet with **zero activity**
- Wallet with **very sparse activity** over years
- Wallet with **extremely high activity** (power user, market maker)
- Chains where Codex backfill is still in progress (Codex exposes backfill state for some aggregates)
- Filters that hide all events on a page (Codex notes that cursor pages can be empty due to filtering)

#### Example tests

- **Cursor stability test:**
  - Fetch a page with cursor `A`
  - Insert a new event at the top via a fixture or mock
  - Fetch again with cursor `A` and assert the same page contents (no duplication or skipping)
- **Merge ordering test:**
  - Simulate events across `eth-mainnet` and `polygon-mainnet`
  - Assert that the combined timeline is ordered strictly by `timestamp` and `blockNumber`

**Common failure:** ignoring the “empty page” case with filtered feeds, leading to broken infinite scroll. Always respect provider cursors even when a page has zero visible events.

Designing a trading‑grade wallet history API is fundamentally about **how you merge and present enriched on‑chain data**, not how you parse raw logs. By pairing a clean internal schema, cursor‑based pagination, and Codex’s wallet and event APIs, you can ship reliable, high‑performance wallet timelines **without** building your own indexers or maintaining fragile blockchain ETL.

## Top 5 Crypto Data APIs for Token-Aware Apps Beyond CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap

Source: https://www.codex.io/blog/best-crypto-data-apis-onchain
Published: 2026-09-27
Author: Codex

When you move from simple price tickers to full token-aware trading, wallet, or prediction market apps, CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap stop being enough.

You need:

- Real-time onchain balances and transfers
- Holders and wallet analytics
- Liquidity and DEX swap visibility
- Prediction market events, markets, trades, and positions

This ranked roundup focuses on **product and engineering teams** building:

- High-traffic trading terminals and social trading apps
- Multi-chain wallets and portfolio dashboards
- DeFi and NFT analytics platforms
- Prediction-market frontends and quant tools

We rank the **top 5 crypto data APIs beyond CoinGecko/CoinMarketCap** based on:

- Depth of **onchain data** (tokens, wallets, transfers, swaps)
- Coverage of **prediction markets**
- Latency and throughput for **trading-grade UX**
- Ease of integration for production apps

Along the way, we’ll clarify a crucial distinction: **where generalized market data ends and trading-grade onchain data begins**, and which API combinations make sense for different product strategies.

> If you want a deeper comparison of traditional market-data vendors, see this guide: [What Is the CoinGecko API? Market Data, On-Chain Coverage and Product Fit](https://www.codex.io/blog/what-is-the-coingecko-api-market-data-on-chain-coverage-and-product-fit).

### Generalized Market Data vs Trading-Grade On-Chain Data

Before we rank providers, it’s important to define the line.

#### What generalized crypto market data APIs give you

Most "crypto data" APIs (including [CoinGecko and CoinMarketCap](https://www.codex.io/blog/best-crypto-data-apis-for-trading-apps-coingecko-coinmarketcap-token-metrics-and), plus vendors like Twelve Data or Finage) focus on:

- Prices and tickers across centralized exchanges
- OHLCV candles for charting
- Basic market metadata (symbol, name, rank)
- Aggregate volume and market cap

They’re ideal when:

- Your interface is CEX-centric
- You only need reference prices
- You aren’t tracking wallets, token transfers, or onchain liquidity

#### Where trading-grade onchain data begins

Trading-grade onchain data APIs go much deeper:

- **Wallet-level state:** balances, transfer history, approvals
- **Token semantics:** holders, token metadata, scam filtering
- **DEX/liquidity:** swaps, pools, liquidityUsd, TVL-like stats
- **Cross-chain indexing:** normalized views across 60–80+ networks
- **Prediction markets:** markets, events, trades, positions, PnL
- **Performance:** sub-second latency, high request throughput, reorg handling

This is the territory where **Codex, The Graph, QuickNode, Tatum, and native venue APIs like Polymarket** compete.

### 1. Codex – Best Overall for Token-Aware Trading, Wallet, and Prediction-Market Apps

Codex is a specialized **blockchain data infrastructure** provider focused on trading-grade token and prediction market data.

- **Coverage:** 80+ networks, 70M+ tokens, 700M+ wallets
- **Customers:** Coinbase, TradingView, Uniswap, Magic Eden, Rainbow, MoonPay, Farcaster, pump.fun and others
- **Core value:** "Fastest and most reliable" onchain token + prediction market data in a **single GraphQL-style API**

#### What Codex does

Codex ingests, enriches, and normalizes raw blockchain data at scale, delivering:

- **Token prices** (USD and native), including real-time and historical
- **Trading-ready charts:** OHLC, candles, volume
- **Aggregated metrics:** liquidityUsd, volume, unique wallets, TVL-like stats
- **Wallet-aware views:** balances, holders, transfers across chains
- **Scam filtering + metadata:** labels, risk signals, launchpad support
- **Prediction markets (beta):** markets, events, trades, trader analytics across Polymarket and Kalshi

It’s built for apps where **latency and correctness are non-negotiable**:

- Portfolio dashboards and multi-chain wallets

Codex’s prediction-market docs highlight a stark performance difference: **1,000+ requests/second** vs around **30 req/s** for [Polymarket’s native API](https://www.codex.io/blog/polymarket-api) and **20 req/s** for Kalshi’s. That’s a clear signal of trading-grade engineering.

#### Who Codex is ideal for

Codex is the best single-vendor option when you need:

- **Tokens + prediction markets in one API**

If you’re a Series A+ startup or enterprise wanting one trusted data layer for **trading, wallets, and prediction markets**, Codex is engineered for that.

#### Where Codex falls short

Honest limitations:

- **Less focused on raw node access:** If you primarily want low-level RPC or custom event streams, a node provider may still be needed.

#### How Codex fits in your stack

For many token-aware apps, a simple pattern is:

- Use **Codex** as the **primary onchain + market data layer**
- Optionally add a reference-price API (e.g., CoinGecko) for redundancy

This consolidates most **token, wallet, and prediction-market data** into one trading-grade API.

### 2. The Graph – Best Decentralized Open Layer for Token Analytics and Protocol Metrics

The Graph is the leading **decentralized indexing protocol**. Developers build "subgraphs" that transform chain events into custom APIs.

- **Coverage:** powers apps on 60+ chains
- **Token API (beta):** Ethereum, Arbitrum, BSC, Polygon, Optimism, Base

#### What The Graph does

The Graph offers two main pieces for token-aware apps:

- **Subgraphs:** Custom, protocol-specific indexers for anything onchain (DEX swaps, NFTs, lending activity, etc.)
- **Token API:** A standardized API for tokens and wallets across key EVM chains

The Token API covers:

- Balances and transaction histories
- Token holders and transfer history
- Pricing and DEX swap data

The Graph team emphasizes that standardized subgraphs make metrics like **TVL and protocol revenue consistent across protocols**, reducing reconciliation work.

#### Who The Graph is ideal for

The Graph is the best fit when you:

- Want **open, decentralized infra** rather than purely centralized SaaS
- Need **protocol-level analytics** (TVL, revenue, user counts)
- Are comfortable designing and maintaining subgraphs or using community ones

Data/quant teams and analytics products often use The Graph as a **foundation**, then add more specialized APIs on top.

#### Where The Graph falls short

Limitations to keep in mind:

- **Token API still in beta:** Limited chain coverage (mostly large EVMs); evolving feature set.
- **Latency and throughput depend on deployment:** Not packaged as a single "trading-grade" SaaS the way Codex is.
- **Prediction markets not first-class:** You’ll need to index prediction protocols yourself or use a specialized API.

#### How The Graph fits in your stack

A common pattern:

- Use **The Graph** for **deep protocol analytics** and custom metrics

For example, a DeFi dashboard could:

- Pull protocol TVL and revenue from The Graph

### 3. QuickNode – Best for High-Throughput Node Access and Event Streams
